findings.title: Recurring failure: NullReferenceException in ContactSync
findings.description: The same failure fingerprint (8471ee8006b8254b) occurred 6 times. At least one occurrence was synchronous, so the user's operation was rolled back and an error was shown.
observedFacts: Exception: System.NullReferenceException (error code -2147220956).
Message: Object reference not set to an instance of an object.
Plug-in types: Contoso.Plugins.ContactSync. Messages: Update. Tables: contact.
Distinct request IDs: 6; distinct correlation IDs: 6.
Top user frames: Contoso.Plugins.ContactSync.ResolvePrimaryContact(Entity order) → Contoso.Plugins.ContactSync.Execute(IServiceProvider serviceProvider)
calculatedMetrics: Rate over its active span: 0.7/h.
possibleExplanations: Error code -2147220956 (0x80040224) usually means an unhandled exception escaped the plug-in code rather than being raised on purpose.

A NullReferenceException in plug-in code often means an expected attribute, image, lookup or context value was missing for this execution (for example, an attribute that isn't in Target on every Update).
recommendedSteps: Open the failure group and compare the original exception text and trace output of the first and latest occurrences.
Check whether the first occurrence lines up with a deployment, a configuration change or a data import.
Reproduce the failure in a non-production environment with the same message, table and input.

findings.title: Slow sync execution: PriceCalculator on Update
findings.description: 5 of 5 measured executions took at least the sync threshold of 2,000 ms. 2 came within reach of the 2-minute synchronous timeout.
observedFacts: Plug-in type: Contoso.Plugins.PriceCalculator; message: Update; mode: Sync; tables: quote.
Slowest execution: 112,500 ms. Executions in group: 5, with a duration: 5.
calculatedMetrics: Share at or above the threshold: 100%.
Average 45,020 ms, median 3,100 ms.
Note: sample of 5 is below 20: 95th percentile not reported.
possibleExplanations: Common causes of slow steps include external HTTP calls, retrieving many records or columns, per-record queries in a loop, and lock contention with concurrent operations. The traces alone don't show which applies.
Synchronous steps add their duration to the user's save time; work that doesn't need to block the user could move to an asynchronous step.
recommendedSteps: Read the trace output of the slowest executions for timing markers, and add timing traces around external calls and queries if there are none.
Check whether the slow executions cluster at certain times (bulk jobs, integrations) or are spread evenly.
Prioritise this step: synchronous executions over 2 minutes are cancelled by the platform.

findings.title: Failures propagating through 6 causal chains: OrderSubmit (depth 1) → ContactSync (depth 2)
findings.description: 6 correlation IDs each link failures from OrderSubmit (depth 1) → ContactSync (depth 2), between 2026-10-26 05:00:00 UTC and 2026-10-26 13:05:00 UTC.
observedFacts: Chains with this shape: 6; failed traces in them: 12; all traces in them: 12.
Example correlation IDs: [GUID-70], [GUID-71], [GUID-72] and 3 more.
correlationEvidence: [Same causal chain (correlation ID)] The failures in each chain share a correlation ID. This proves they belong to one causal chain, not that they are the same immediate operation.
[Suspected parent/child] In 6 chains, OrderSubmit (depth 1) → ContactSync (depth 2); signals: same correlation ID, depth differs by one, runs inside the other's execution window.
possibleExplanations: A failure in a nested (deeper) synchronous step propagates to the step that triggered it, so one underlying failure can appear as several exceptions in one chain. Start with the deepest failure.
recommendedSteps: Open one of the chains in the Trace explorer (Chain ◀ ▶) and read the failures in order of depth and start time.
Check whether the deepest failure's message appears inside the shallower failures' messages.

findings.title: Suspected recursion: AccountHierarchy on Update at depths 1, 2, 3, 4
findings.description: Within correlation ID [GUID-73], Contoso.Plugins.AccountHierarchy ran for Update at 4 depths.
observedFacts: Executions in the chain: 4; depths: 1, 2, 3, 4; failures: 0.
correlationEvidence: [Same causal chain (correlation ID)] Same correlation ID [GUID-73].
possibleExplanations: A step that updates the record it is registered on (or a related record that triggers it back) re-triggers itself. Dataverse stops such loops at depth 8 with an error.
This can also be legitimate: a hierarchy update that cascades to child records runs the same step at increasing depths.
recommendedSteps: Check whether the step updates attributes that are in its own filtering attributes, and whether it guards with context.Depth.

caveats: Rates are compared per hour of each period. A change in usage volume between the periods changes failure counts too.

limitations: Plug-in trace logs are only written when tracing is enabled, and Dataverse deletes them after a retention period. Missing traces are not evidence that no failures happened.
Correlation ID links traces in one causal chain, which can span several operations and asynchronous continuations. It does not prove that two traces are the same operation.
Parent/child relationships are inferred from depth and timing and are labelled as suspected. Dataverse does not record them.
Heuristic correlations (no shared identifier) are leads to check, not proof of a shared transaction.
Possible explanations are hypotheses that guide the investigation. They are not confirmed root causes.
An execution is only called slow when its recorded duration meets the configured threshold for its execution mode.
